scenarios.name: Optimistic (best case, high productivity, no major surprises)
Most Likely (expected case with normal friction)

nonLabourLines.description: Stripe integration fees / sandbox testing (assumed negligible direct cost, transactional fees excluded)
Cloud hosting/staging environment setup (CI/CD, staging infra) - indicative allowance
Legacy Oracle data migration tooling/licensing (assumed one-time)
Contingency buffer for third-party/API costs (email service, search, tracing tools)

assumptions: The rate card is a PLACEHOLDER: only one generic 'Team member' role at $75/hr with 1 FTE is defined. No real roles (e.g. developer, QA, PM, designer) or differentiated rates exist yet. All costs below are indicative only and MUST be revisited once the client assigns real roles and hourly rates to team members.

With only 1 FTE (a single 'Team member') available at 75 USD/hr, and 24 backlog items totalling 189 story points, the team is severely understaffed relative to the backlog. Assuming ~1 point = ~15 hours of effort (a common rough translation for a small full-stack Angular/API team), total estimated effort is ~2835-2880 hours, i.e. ~1.4-1.5 years of continuous solo full-time work for one person, ignoring vacation, illness, or context-switching overhead.

No historical actuals (real spend data) are available for this project yet. This estimate is built purely from backlog point sizing and the placeholder rate card, not from empirical velocity or cost data. Actuals should replace these assumptions as soon as real sprints are completed.

Story points were converted to hours using a flat ratio of ~15 hours/point as a rough industry heuristic for a single generalist handling full-stack + testing + deployment work solo; this is a rough approximation given no team velocity history exists.

Because there is only one FTE, all work is inherently serialized; the point estimate assumes no parallelism, so the 3 scenarios reflect variance in per-task efficiency and rework/surprises (e.g., legacy migration, Stripe integration) rather than differences in team size.
Non-labour costs are indicative placeholders for infrastructure, migration tooling and third-party services; actual figures depend on vendor selection not yet made.
Priority breakdown cost was apportioned from total labour cost in the most-likely scenario, weighted by each task's story points within its priority group.

PW-8 (Legacy data migration, 21 points) and PW-7 (Payment integration, 13 points) are the highest-risk, highest-effort items and are the primary drivers of the pessimistic scenario due to potential data quality issues and third-party integration friction.

Given the single-FTE constraint, delivering the full backlog end-to-end in a reasonable timeframe is unrealistic without additional hires; this estimate assumes the client either accepts a much longer timeline or plans to add headcount/roles to the rate card before work begins.
input.reasoning: Backlog was translated to hours using story points x ~15 hrs/point (a rough proxy given no velocity data), producing ~2835-2880 hours of total effort across all 24 tasks. Since the only defined role is a single 'Team member' at $75/hr with 1 FTE, all labour was costed under that one line, making the total labour cost roughly hours x $75. Three scenarios (P20/P50/P80) reflect uncertainty in per-task effort due to the high-risk items (legacy migration, Stripe payments, RBAC, multi-currency) and the fact that a lone generalist absorbs all delivery risk with no parallelism or specialization. Non-labour costs are small, indicative placeholders for infra, migration tooling and third-party service allowances. Priority breakdown apportions the most-likely total labour cost across Urgent/High/Medium/Low buckets by summing story points per priority and scaling proportionally. Given the severe FTE-to-backlog mismatch, the estimate strongly assumes the client will add real, differentiated roles to the rate card before delivery starts; until then, all numbers are directional only.

reductions.description: Descope Low-priority items (PW-12 Support ticket submission, PW-18 Admin back-office, PW-19 Usage analytics, PW-23 Contract tests, PW-24 Decommission legacy portal) from this phase and defer to a later release; total 39 points removed.
reductions.effect: Removes ~585 hours (39 pts x 15 hrs) of Team member time at $75/hr from scope, reducing total labour cost and shortening delivery timeline by roughly 3-4 months given single-FTE staffing.

reductions.description: Simplify Multi-currency support (PW-14, 13 pts) to a single-currency MVP (USD only) for launch, adding EUR/PLN later once core portal is stable.
reductions.effect: Cuts estimated effort for this task roughly in half (from ~195 hrs to ~90 hrs), saving ~105 hrs at $75/hr; reduces integration and FX-rate complexity risk in the pessimistic scenario.

reductions.description: Reduce Accessibility pass (PW-15, 8 pts) scope to only the customer-facing critical flows (login, dashboard, invoices, payments) rather than all screens, deferring back-office/admin screens until PW-18 is built.
reductions.effect: Cuts ~80 hrs of effort at $75/hr by narrowing the WCAG audit surface for this phase.

reductions.description: Add real, differentiated roles (e.g. mid-level developer, QA, PM) to the rate card and increase headcount beyond 1 FTE before committing to a delivery date, rather than trying to compress the single-FTE timeline with overtime.
reductions.effect: This does not reduce total dollar cost directly but prevents an unrealistic single-person delivery risk; it converts calendar-time risk into a staffing decision. Strongly recommended before finalizing any fixed-price commitment.

reductions.description: Defer Legacy data migration (PW-8, 21 pts) to a follow-on project phase after the new portal launches with manual/CSV import fallback, since it is the single largest and riskiest item.
reductions.effect: Removes ~315 hrs (21 pts x 15 hrs) from this phase's labour cost and eliminates the biggest driver of the pessimistic-scenario cost variance; migration can be scoped and priced separately once legacy schema quality is better understood.
